en: Now, SSH hardening is about more than just
using Fail2Ban. It's also about, for
example, not even allowing root user access
or password-based access. Because at the
moment, and that's really important to
understand, if I were to open a new terminal
on my Mac or on your Windows machine,
you could also connect to that VPS by using
SSH as we did before, and then your username
root, or in my case, Max, and then add the
IP.
And not use that SSH key. So I'm not adding
-i as we did before.
And if I hit Enter, I'm asked for my
password. Now in the past, I didn't know
what my root user password is, but I know
the password for my Max user.
And if I enter that, boom,
I'm connected.
And that is a little security issue here
because that means that of course,
theoretically, people could try to brute
force their way into that or guess your
password. And sure, Fail2Ban makes it a bit
harder, but it's not impossible.
And for that reason, you typically wanna
disable password authentication entirely,
forcing people to log in with that SSH key.
And you typically also wanna disable root
login so that people have to go through a
user who does not have full root access by
default.
So installing and running Fail2Ban is one
important step, but not the only one. We
also wanna go through further SSH hardening
to make connecting via SSH more difficult.
And for that, we wanna tweak the SSH
configuration on our VPS because that
controls how other people, other machines
like our MacBook, our Windows machine can
connect to it.
And to do that, we use
again the nano text editor and we could now
access /etc/ssh/
/sshd_config, and that gives us access to
the configuration file for SSH on that VPS.
Now you can edit this file, you can
absolutely do that,
but a better pattern is to create a
dedicated config file
that will be merged with this config file
and override parts of it. So that's what
we'll do here. So I'll hit Ctrl+X to close
this,
And I'll then
again use sudo nano, same path, but add
.d
after the config file name. That's important
because that is now a directory with that
name next to this config file,
forward slash,
and then any name of your choice, but a
common choice is 99-hardening.conf. Now what
will that do?
That will add a new file with that name
in that path. And I chose this name because
in that sshd_config.d folder,
Files will be ordered alphabetically. So
this naturally will come last. At the
moment, it should be the only file, but if
we had more files, it will come last.
And the files in that folder will override
the base configuration and the topmost file
will have the highest priority. So 99 will
have a pretty low priority. So using 99
hardening.conf here simply allows us to have
some config which we could override by in
the future adding a
8-something file in front of it.
But in general, the file name is up to you.
All.conf files in that folder will be
merged with the base config and will
overwrite the base config regarding the
settings they touch.
So if I hit Enter, I enter a brand new empty
file because this file is literally just
created in this moment. It didn't exist
before.
And we can paste some settings in there and
you'll find those settings attached, of
course.
Now, what do these settings do?
Pub key authentication,
yes,
ensures that we can connect via SSH to this
VPS using an SSH key, which is the method
we've been using.
Password authentication, no, disables
password-based authentication though. And
that's big and important because in the past
we could connect via passwords
And as mentioned, that's not perfectly
secure. So we typically wanna disable this,
which is just what this setting does.
KBD interactive authentication is a
different authentication mechanism approach
we're not using here, so we disable it.
Permit empty passwords, we disable so that
users can't even try to connect without a
password.
So
that kind of goes together with disabling
password authentication overall.
Permit_root_login is another important one.
This ensures that we won't be able to
connect as the root user anymore. If you
have an ongoing connection as the root user,
that will keep on going, it will not be
terminated, but you won't be able to
establish a new one. You can only connect
via your user instead, the max user in my
case.
So permit_root_login set to no is a very
important setting because it ensures that
there isn't even a theoretical way of
connecting as a root user to your VPS,
which is good because root users have
unlimited power on the VPS.
Max auth tries is self-explanatory, I guess.
And X11 forwarding is another interface
we're disabling here,
which could be used for connecting some
graphical user interfaces to the VPS, which
is something we're not using. If you want to
connect a monitor or something like that.
Allow users, here you simply list the users
that should be able to connect. And in my
case, I only want to allow Max.
So now I'll quit this with Ctrl+X and hit Y
to save and hit Enter to confirm the file
name.
And with that done, nothing will happen
because we changed the config, but it will
not have been applied yet.
To apply it,
you wanna run sudo sshd -t.
